items.prompt: Per L2, what's the actual test for whether a function has a single responsibility?
choices: Whether the function is under 10 lines long

Whether there's only one distinct reason someone might need to modify it — a function can do several literal steps and still have a single responsibility if they all serve one cohesive, independently-changing purpose
Whether the function has a single return statement
Whether the function calls fewer than three other functions
items.explanation: Line count and literal step count are explicitly rejected as the test — the real criterion is distinct reasons to change, which is why a short function can still violate SRP (if it bundles two independent concerns) and a longer one might not (if every step serves one cohesive, single-reason purpose).

items.prompt: Per L2, is the correct responsibility boundary for a given piece of code the same in every codebase?
choices: Yes — SRP has one universally correct boundary for any given code shape

No — whether two things count as "distinct reasons to change" depends on the actual codebase's context (who owns what, what changes on independent schedules); the same code can have a correct single responsibility in one context and a real violation in another
Yes, but only for backend code, not frontend code
No, because SRP is purely a matter of personal coding style preference
items.explanation: L2 explicitly frames SRP as a judgment call informed by context, not a universal rule — the same validation-rules-and-error-messages example is given as correctly unified in a small system and correctly split in a larger one, depending on actual ownership and change patterns.

items.prompt: A function is split into `getEmailField`, `isValidEmailFormat`, and `validateEmail`, where each only ever exists to feed the next. Per L2, is this a good application of SRP?
choices: Yes — more, smaller functions always better satisfy single responsibility

No — none of these three pieces have an independent reason to change from each other; splitting adds indirection (three names to track, extra jumps to read) with no corresponding benefit, which is the overcorrection failure mode
Yes, because each function technically does only one thing
No, because functions should never call other functions
items.explanation: L2 explicitly uses this as the overcorrection example — the test isn't whether code CAN be split further (almost anything can), it's whether splitting lets two genuinely independent kinds of future change happen without touching each other's code, which this example doesn't achieve.

items.prompt: In L3's incident, an engineer making a PDF-layout change accidentally also broke billing calculation. Per L3, what was the actual root cause?
choices: The engineer was careless and should have been more attentive

The billing-sensitive rate logic and the layout-only PDF rendering lived in the same method with no structural separation, making a stray edit to unrelated code an easy, low-friction mistake to make by accident
The rebrand request itself was poorly specified
There was no real root cause; this kind of incident is unpreventable
items.explanation: L3 explicitly separates the immediate mistake (a stray edit) from the structural root cause (billing logic and layout logic sharing a method with no boundary between them) — the fix targets the structural cause, since individual mistakes are common and expected, not rare exceptions to design around.

items.prompt: Per L3's first failure mode, does splitting `MonthlyReportGenerator` into three classes make the billing-calculation bug from the incident impossible to repeat?
choices: Yes — the split alone completely eliminates any possibility of this class of bug

No — the split reduces the CHANCE of an accidental cross-responsibility edit, but doesn't make it impossible; the real protection is the combination of separation AND a dedicated billing test suite that would catch an incorrect rate change regardless of which file it happened in
No, the split has no effect on this risk at all
Yes, but only if the classes are also renamed
items.explanation: L3 is explicit that the split reduces risk structurally (billing logic isn't visually adjacent to layout code anymore) but isn't a complete guarantee on its own — a dedicated, protected test suite for the billing logic is the piece that would actually catch a wrong rate value regardless of how or where it was introduced.

items.prompt: Implement `countDistinctReasons(changeLog)`, where `changeLog` is an array of past commit reasons (strings) touching a given function, e.g. `['validation rule', 'validation rule', 'response format']`. Return the count of DISTINCT reasons — a simple, concrete way to check L2's test against a function's real change history.

tests.description: all changes for the same reason count as 1
two distinct reasons are counted separately
an empty history has zero distinct reasons

items.explanation: This is a literal, checkable version of L2's test applied retrospectively: if a function's real commit history shows more than one distinct reason recurring, that's concrete evidence (not just a hypothetical) that it's bundling independent responsibilities — exactly the kind of signal that could have flagged the MonthlyReportGenerator's billing-and-layout coupling before the incident in L3, if its change history had been examined this way.
